speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That when the House adjourns for its summer recess it shall stand adjourned until October 22, 1969, provided always that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with Her Majesty's Government, that the public interest requires that the House should meet at an earlier time during the adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give notice that he is so satisfied, and thereupon the House shall meet at the time stated in such notice, and shall transact its business as if it had been duly adjourned to that time; and
That, in the event of Mr. Speaker being unable to act owing to illness or other cause, the Deputy Speaker or the Deputy Chairman of Committees shall act in his stead for the purpose of reconvening the House.
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to support the motion. I propose to move that the motion be amended by deleting the words "October 22" where they appear in the second line and substituting therefore the words "September 22".
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
I rise to present this amendment, Sir, on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. The effect of the amendment is clear: We should resume parliament not on October 22 but a month earlier on September 22. In view of the accumulation of serious problems facing this country it is immature and irresponsible for the government to send parliament off on a three-month vacation. I think the people of this country will be scandalized at the casual and apparently carefree attitude adopted by the government toward the problems of the country and its responsibilities to find solutions to those problems.
I do not deny for a moment that Members of Parliament are as entitled to a holiday as anybody else, and it must be clear that a good many members of parliament are rather tired today. Furthermore, we all have important work to do in our constituencies and elsewhere. However, there is no reason in the world that parliament should shut down until October 22. The people of Canada will regard a three-month holiday as rather too much of a good thing and as representing a very blase attitude toward our responsibilities.
I want to make it very clear where the responsibility for this proposed action rests. The government, and the government alone, is insisting on a prolonged adjournment and we on this side, at least those in this party, disassociate ourselves completely from this casual irresponsibility of the government. They are like kids who want to play truant from their responsibilities.
There is no reason-
Oh, oh.
I would suggest, Sir-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

I would suggest that my hon. friends save their breath and their voices because if they are disturbed by what I have

said so far they may need their lungs more for what I am going to say later.
There is no reason for the government to keep parliament shut down for almost three months, except the complete disdain of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet for this institution. They do not like questions, they do not like free debate, and they find parliament a nuisance and an inconvenience. They cannot quite do away with the institution altogether but they impose rules which will give them complete control over it, and they will keep it adjourned just as long as they can.
In view of the kind of parliament envisaged by this government and its supporters in the house, a parliament which meets relatively briefly to endorse the decrees of Caesar after very cursory discussion, it is clear that the attitude of the government and its supporters toward the institutions of government in this country, the attitude of the federal Liberal party, particularly those in this government, differs very little from the views expressed by General de Gaulle-a great soldier, a great patriot, a great man, but hardly a democrat as we understand democracy in this country. It is not for me to suggest what kind of government or government institutions are suitable for France.
Why are you talking about France?

As I say, Mr. Speaker, it is not for me to say what is suitable for France. But it is coming through loud and clear all the time that this government envisages periodic elections and government in the meantime by press conference and pre-sessions of parliament. It is true we do not have a president, but a rose smells just as sweet by any other name-or a carnation, as far as that is concerned.
Hear, hear!
So does an egg plant.
Oh, oh!
Now we are told that parliament is to meet toward the end of October.
What year?
That was a great contribution, Hogarth.

I do not know. It might be put off for another year. In view of the problems that face the country, there is no adequate excuse for this action. The government
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
says it needs this time to get its legislative program ready for the next session. This is one of the most incredible explanations that could possibly be put forward at this point in time. The government was elected in June of 1968. This session of parliament began on September 12. It was stated in the Speech from the Throne, and it has been repeated numerous times by members of the cabinet and by the propagandists of the Liberal party, that the present session of parliament should be regarded as merely a "clean-up session", that the government, in its orderly and efficient way, wanted to tidy up all the legislative items that were hanging over from the Pearson administration. This session of parliament was chiefly to clear the decks for the new exciting legislation that would usher in the just society.
After spending a whole session of parliament dealing with legislative left-overs from the Pearson government, are the members of this cabinet seriously trying to pretend that they do not have a program ready for the next session of parliament?

They do not have a
program.

That explanation, Mr. Speaker, is just not believable, unless the government is more inept and dishonest with the people than we feared. It should be mentioned in passing that there were items, some of them very important, in the Speech from the Throne which the government has not yet brought forward in legislative form.
Due to filibuster.
I am not impressed by that interjection, Mr. Speaker. We hear all this talk about filibuster, and now the government is asking the house to recess for three months and to meet on October 22.
What a joke!

It is comforting to have a government supporter show how hollow all this talk has been. What has happened to the educational television bill? What has become of that hardy, old perennial, the Canada Development Corporation? The government removed from the order paper the item having to do with the Indian Claims Commission, thus welshing once more on the understanding given to the Indian people. They have now decided to appoint a commissioner who, in effect, will decide whether there should be

Motion to Adjourn House a claims commission and, if so, what claims will be considered worthy of being heard by it.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
What has become of this magnificently efficient cabinet structure, organized so finely that decisions roll out just as though they came from a computer? What has happened to it, Mr. Speaker? I suppose someone will tell us that committees are meeting in September and that it is a good idea to have the committees free to meet when parliament is adjourned. That is not the same reason that has been given to us so far in any explanation as to why the house is not meeting earlier. We have been told that the government needs time between sessions to get its program ready. This is very difficult to believe of this highly structured, highly organized, computer-like administration.
We have been told in the course of recent days that the government has urgent and important business to bring before the house when the session resumes. Some of it is even said to be highly controversial. This, we were told, was why they needed the weapon of rule 75c. Let us come back here in September and let us see that important legislation.
Hear, hear.

If the government is going to chop off debate when we start to consider legislation, I suggest it is going to be pretty hard to add to this more subtle form of closure by keeping parliament adjourned for long periods. I know how unappealing the idea is to the finer sensibilities of the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, but is it not time that the parliament of Canada began to deal with specific solutions to the disgraceful situation in this country regarding poverty? The entire field of anti-poverty measures has been left completely untouched by this government. I suppose they do not want to get their hands dirty.
We were told there has been a review of the whole social welfare system in Canada. Where is it and what is it? When will we see it? What new solutions does the government have to propose? These are questions that directly relate to the thousands of people who are hopelessly trapped by poverty.
While this government relaxes during the month of September, many young people will be prevented from returning to school. Many
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House will not be able to take advantage of educational training programs because they have not been able to get work and will not be in a financial position to do so. For every day that this government delays the introduction of effective anti-poverty measures, thousands of Canadians sink deeper and deeper into poverty.
Who is the author?

We were told that the water act is supposed to be ready in the course of the summer. Why cannot we start work on that? What about the government's own public service pensioners? Are they going to continue to be put off while parliament is in recess? What about the veterans of our armed services? These people and others must be near the top of the priority scheme of the government, if there is one. The people of Canada can only assume that the just society is just a cynical piece of hypocrisy.
Hear, hear.

Are we to stay out until October 22 and leave the country's anti-inflationary program to the tender mercies of this government? Then there is supposed to be legislation relating to corporate disclosure. Why can we not deal with that?
There is no need for me to go on longer detailing the list of things that need urgent consideration. All I will say in closing is that this motion to recess until the 22nd day of October may be all right for the hon. gentlemen opposite who consider this institution to be of small importance, and who consider the important decisions as being those taken by the government and not those taken by parliament. It may suit them fine. But I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it will appear reprehensible in the eyes of the Canadian people, and I call upon the house to support the amendment I propose and to reject the date proposed by the government this morning.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of supporting the amendment which has just been moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). Indeed had he not moved such an amendment I would have moved one along similar lines because I am in full accord with the proposition that parliament ought not to recess for three months and that we ought to be back in our places by at least September 22.
[Mr. Stanfield.l
Why not earlier?
Why not?
Why did your members leave?
So did yours.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has the floor.

I can understand the Prime Minister's petulance. He probably has not had much sleep.
I want to point out that the government motion that this house recess until October 22 completely destroys the credibility of the government. For months they have been trying to convince the Canadian people that parliament has been preventing them from passing much needed legislation, that they were obstructed in some way, or hindered in bringing in legislation which would completely revolutionize Canadian society. Now they have so little to present to parliament that they are suggesting parliament take a three-months' holiday.
In the house on July 8, as reported on page 10982 of Hansard, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) said that if there had not been prolonged debate on certain matters, particularly the omnibus bill on the Criminal Code, the government would have proposed many important measures. Well, if there are important measures which the government desires to see passed, there are two things we could have done. We could have continued to sit on into July instead of planning to adjourn on June 27. There would have been no objection on the part of opposition members to sitting during the summer months in order to discharge their responsibilities. We have done it before.
The second thing the government could have done was to call for the reconvening of parliament early in September, immediately after Labour Day. But the government has not done either one of these things. We have dealt with no legislation at all since the first two or three days in July, and now the government suggests it has nothing to put before parliament and that there is no need to bring members back before October 22. I would remind the house that if we start a new session on October 22 with the debate on the address no legislation will be dealt with until the month of November. This means a period
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
of almost four months during which no legislation will have been dealt with by parliament.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
On July 22 the Prime Minister gave an interview before the television cameras, where he seems to prefer to carry on most of his debates because the cameras cannot interrupt, ask questions or talk back. At that time he said that the people were confronted with a "do-nothing parliament". I would point out that parliament has been very busy. It has been busy most of the time trying to get the government to take action on the important problems that are facing the country. But the country is confronted with a "do-nothing government". The best proof that it is a "do-nothing government" is that it does not even want to bring parliament back until October 22 because it has nothing to put before it.
I would ask Your Honour whether you can imagine a course of action more inconsistent than this. The government brings in rules changes, ostensibly for the purpose of streamlining parliament. But we now find that the only purpose of streamlining parliament is not to enable parliament to do more business but to give its members a longer holiday. Closure was not introduced so that the government could streamline parliament and deal with the important issues of the day; it was introduced so that we could have shorter sessions of parliament, so that the government could get parliament out of the road.
I said that the government's credibility had been destroyed because it had talked about legislation it wanted to put before the house and had not done so. Where is this legislation? Why is it not put before us? Why does the government not bring it down, either now or in September? The time has come for the government to stop bluffing and to start performing. The time has come to put up or shut up. To use an old fishermen's phrase, the time has come to "fish or cut bait". There is also an old printer's phrase that is apt, Mr. Speaker, but our parliamentary rules would not allow me to use it.
The real fact of the matter is that this government, particularly the Prime Minister, does not want parliament around at all. Parliament is an unnecessary encumbrance, a continuing embarrassment. Hon. members opposite would like us to go home because the opposition has become a nuisance. The opposition keeps asking questions that the government cannot answer. The opposition
Motion to Adjourn House keeps insisting that the government state its policies in regard to a whole host of matters, but the government has no policies and does not like to admit it. So the simple solution is to send members of parliament home and to keep them at home for as long as possible.
The government claims that it needs time to formulate its policies and to prepare its parliamentary program. If the President of the Privy Council is right and there is a lot of legislation that the government wanted to get through, then surely that legislation must be ready now. Therefore parliament could meet in September and deal with it while the cabinet meets to prepare any other legislation the government has in mind.
The government does not need three months to sit in an ivory tower to consider problems that have been before it for a long time. These are problems in regard to which the government has appointed task forces, committees and commissions. The desks of ministers opposite must be piled high with reports. If the government has no policies or legislation, then it should say so honestly. Let it say to the members of this house: "We are not ready because we have no legislation. We want a little time to think up some new answers to old problems, so please go away and leave us alone." That would at least be an honest attitude to take.
What the government is doing is telling the public, on the one hand, that there are many things the government wants to do but which an obstructive opposition keeps it from doing. On the other hand, when the government does have a chance to put legislation before the house, it tells parliament: "We don't want you around at all". The motion moved by the government to recess the house till October 22 demonstrates that the government is made up of phonies who are trying to fool the people of this country, and I want to tell the government that it will not get away with it.
During the course of the interview on July 22 to which I referred a few moments ago the Prime Minister said: "I think the greatest danger in this country was not closure, but the feeling of the people that the government was irrelevant, that things were happening, whether pollution, or housing, or moonshots, or urban slums, that parliament was not dealing with.
Hear, hear.

I hear a few backbenchers opposite applauding. I notice that the majority of the
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House government members have the uncomfortable feeling that the matters which the Prime Minister says parliament was not dealing with are the very things that the government has not been dealing with. Has parliament not been dealing with pollution? Certainly opposition members have raised the question of pollution on every conceivable occasion. But what has the government done in connection with pollution?
Nothing.

It is almost two years since I heard the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen), at a time when he was minister of health and welfare, make a resounding speech in the house about legislation that he was just ready to bring down and which, to quote his words, was going to give Canada pure water and clean air. Where is that legislation? Never has there been as much pollution in Canada as there is today.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I would take the liberty of bringing to the attention of hon. members that it is extremely difficult to follow the speech of the hon. member.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)
I do not mind the interruptions, Mr. Speaker. There is an old saying in the north that if you throw a stone into a pack of dogs and one yelps you have hit something.
Explain.

Never has the problem of pollution been so acute as it is today. Never have the people of this country been so conscious of what we are doing to the environment of the Canadian people. Where is the water act? Where is the legislation to deal with pollution? We have had no legislation, We have not got pure water or clean air. All we have had is a lot of hot air.
Hear, hear.

When the Prime Minister has the unmitigated gall to say that parliament is not dealing with pollution, the responsibility rests right on his doorstep because he and his party are the people who should be introducing legislation to deal with the matter.
[Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Island) .1
The second matter that the Prime Minister said parliament is not dealing with is housing. We are very conscious of the fact that parliament is not dealing adequately with housing. As a matter of fact, the government did nothing about housing until the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), when he was the Prime Minister's senior cabinet minister and desk-mate, finally got so frustrated that he gave the Prime Minister a kick in the place where the Prime Minister was going to kick the little boy in Regina.
Oh, oh!

We finally got some legislation. It is inadequate legislation, but that is the only time the government moved with any commendable speed. The other matter the Prime Minister referred to that parliament was not dealing with was moonshots. I do not know what the Prime Minister wants us to do about moonshots, Mr. Speaker, but something which concerns the human race even more than moonshots is the danger of a nuclear holocaust that could destroy the human race.
As far back as March the Prime Minister said that the government would follow the question of the Safeguard A.B.M. system closely. He said that if Canada thought it would escalate the nuclear arms race the government would express its disapproval to the United States and to the world. On the other hand, if the government felt the Safeguard system would be of value it might be prepared to participate and its decision would be made known to parliament and to the Canadian people. Months have elapsed. The other day I asked the Prime Minister whether a decision had been reached. He said no.
In the course of the next few days the United States Senate will make a decision. The majority leader of the Senate says that in all probability the construction of the Safeguard A.B.M. system will be approved by that body. Instead of worrying about moonshots, the Prime Minister should be worried about the A.B.M. system. This parliament should have an opportunity to debate that question. We should be able to debate it on the basis of what the government's stated policy is, not on the basis of no comment and no decision.
The Prime Minister said the other day that parliament is not dealing with slum clearance. The only reason it is not dealing with slum clearance is that the government has not put any really useful and effective legislation
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
before the house so that we can deal with the question of slum clearance.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) keeps turning down every proposal on the basis that it is inflationary. Yet we have had no legislation to deal with the problem of inflation. Just two days ago the near-banks of this country raised their interest rates again. This will undoubtedly bring pressure to bear on the chartered banks to increase their rates further. An announcement two days ago indicates that the increasing interest rates for mortgage money has had the effect of reducing housing starts with the distinct possibility that starts this year will not even reach the 197,000 starts of last year.
Where is the legislation to deal with inflation? It took the government almost a year to set up the Prices and Incomes Commission. There has been no legislation on the matter of interest rates. There has been no legislation to implement the report of the Porter Commission to bring the near-banks under the control of the federal government through the Bank Act. There has been no legislation on inflation at all.
The government says that the most pressing problem in Canada today is inflation, yet there is not one piece of legislation before us now. We are going to be sent home until October 22. No legislation can be dealt with until November. Yet the government says inflation is a serious problem. There are many other problems, Mr. Speaker. I need not enumerate them all.
One of the most pressing problems is veterans' pensions. The veterans of this country have been waiting years for the Woods report. Now we have the Woods report. Instead of acting on it, the government is waiting for a white paper. They are going to send the report and the white paper to a committee. We could have had legislation in this session. If the government requested it, every member would stay here to deal with legislation to improve the plight of the veterans.

Where are your
members?
They are coming back on Monday.

The hon. gentleman is worrying
about members. What he should worry about is where the government members were on the day parliament adjourned early for lack of a quorum.
Motion to Adjourn House
There were seven in the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Again it is difficult to hear the hon. member. I think in fairness I should point out that the verbal crossfire is between individual members on both sides of the house.

One of the most serious problems which has not been dealt with by parliament because the government has no program and no policy is the plight of western agriculture. We are being asked to go home only a week before the end of the crop year. We do not know what the government's policy is going to be with respect to assuring the farmers that they will be able to deliver at least five bushels per acre in the present crop year which ends July 31. We have no understanding as to what the government's intentions are with respect to the price the farmer will receive in the new crop year which begins on August 1. We have received no indication from the government as to what its policies are to inject a massive infusion of cash income into the pockets of the western farmers.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
The Prime Minister spent the best part of a week in western Canada talking to the farmers and meeting with various farm groups. When he had finished those discussions, at least he admitted that the farmers need money. When he returned we had a day's debate on this matter. The Prime Minister took no part in it. We had no announcement from the government concerning any policy envisaged for the coming year. The only reference was to legislation passed months ago to provide for cash advances on farm stored grain. Just a week ago I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), when he was Acting Prime Minister, when the government would make a statement concerning its policy in respect of western agriculture. His reply was very clear. He said it would have to be made before the end of the crop year. But we have had no statement.
It is very likely, Mr. Speaker, that important legislation will be required if we are to salvage the economy of western Canada. Next November will be too late. We should either be dealing with that legislation now or should be told by the government that it will have legislation ready for early September. We should be dealing with that legislation.

Hear, hear.
11630	COMMONS
Motion to Adjourn House

I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the plight of western agriculture is not purely a regional matter. The farmers of Saskatchewan alone buy annually about $100 million worth of farm machinery, most of it coming from central Canada. They also buy large quantities of hardware, cars, trucks and other supplies. When agricultural income on the prairies declines by $430 million in a single year, it is only a matter of time until the rest of Canada feels the adverse effects of that decline. Here we have a government which professes to be concerned about the problem of the prairie farmers asking us, on July 25, to go home without any statement from the government about what it is going to do, and not only to go home but to remain at home until October 22 which means that in that period no legislation will be possible to salvage the situation in the prairie provinces.
There are a great many other things with which parliament has not dealt. In closing I wish to say there is only one reason parliament has not dealt with these matters. It is not because there has been obstruction. It is not because we are unwilling to sit here in the summer or come back early in the fall. The only reason parliament has not grappled with the problems that assail the Canadian people is that this government has no policies and no programs. It is completely bankrupt of leadership, and the motion today exposes that fact for all to see.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock this morning, the Liberal majority applied the rule of closure. At 1:20, the sinister rule 75c was imposed upon us again by the Liberal majority and now, at noon today, they propose no more or no less the pure and simple closing down of parliament for three months.
The present government is heaved-handed when it comes to closure, while very serious and urgent problems not only remain unsolved but have not been discussed or introduced by the Liberal administration.
Mr. Speaker, we are about to go on holidays. I am not against holidays for the hon. members, but in all ridings we note that there are some people who do not have the means to take holidays but who have them to pay taxes and allow their member of parliament to go on holidays.

DEBATES	July 25, 1969

You have been on holidays for three weeks already.
Another hon. Member: Some members take ten-month holidays.

I hear a member saying that some members take ten-month holidays. We know that. We see them in the house on holidays, because they are not brave enough to rise and state their opinions. Those people are on holidays for four years. However, they are not on holidays when they have to go and beg for votes which they obtain on false pretences to come here and wear out the seat of their pants in the Canadian parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I am not against taking holidays, even for three months, as was suggested by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald). That would be normal under a normal system, if the legislative program were brought in. As for problems, we solve them from day to day.
Hardly a few days ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) said that we could do nothing for western farmers with regard to their wheat surplus.
The Prime Minister went to Winnipeg and told farmers: You have wheat, sell it. It belongs to you. We have no miracle solution to suggest.
Recently the Prime Minister returned to western Canada where, in some places, he was given a rather stormy welcome. He was even insulted. The Prime Minister then made the following statement: We shall ear-mark $250 million to help western farmers. We shall provide them with those funds without interest until they have sold their crop.
And, in order to project a better image to the farmers, the Minister of Agriculture visited the same regions the following day and told the farmers: We may even ear-mark up to $500 million rather than only $250 million.
Mr. Speaker, in order to get the government to act, will it be absolutely necessary that the Prime Minister be insulted from one end of the country to the other, and that Canada's poor fling insults at him and at the government?
As far as the summer recess is concerned, the motion moved by the President of the Privy Council reads in part as follows:
-provided always that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with Her Majesty's Government, that the public interest requires that the House should meet at an earlier time during the adjournment-
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
-at that time, the house might meet again in September, in August or early in October.
[DOT] (12 noon)
Mr. Speaker, would it not be in the public interest to solve the unemployment problem in Canada in July 1969, in order to assist some 400,000 unemployed who cannot earn a decent and honourable living in their own country?
Mr. Speaker, would the introduction of measures designed to efficiently fight poverty in Canada not serve the public interest? There are many poor people in Canada, Welfare recipients, for instance, write us day in, day out. The Liberal members also get the same kind of letters. Some mothers are utterly crushed because they have to manage to live on a monthly income of $110, $115 or $125. Mothers with five, six, eight or even ten children write to us: We have no security, we are entitled to nothing more than $125 or $135 per month.
Mr. Speaker, would it not be more important for the Prime Minister and the government to present legislation to improve social welfare so that every individual would have the right to life, security and liberty in his own country, that is Canada?
Mr. Speaker, is it more important to go on holidays or to solve these problems? Is it more important to go on holidays than to work at boosting the Canadian economy?
Day after day, the Prime Minister repeats that we have enormous problems to solve. Are we going to leave those problems pending? When the time comes for solving problems, the Prime Minister says exactly what he said recently to the representatives of the provinces: We have no money.
Would it not be more important, during the holidays, to look into the monetary system of Canada, in order to gear it to our opportunities for developing the country?
No, they prefer to move a motion to enable us to take holidays. Meanwhile, all problems remain unsolved and their study is deferred. The provinces complain to the federal government and municipalities complain to provincial governments, yet no solution can be found to those problems.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke earlier of western producers who, according to the Minister of Agriculture, will get up to $500 million in cash, as long as their wheat remains unsold. We are not against western farmers being assisted. We have always supported the measures that are likely to assist western farmers.
Motion to Adjourn House
But, Mr. Speaker, there are farmers in eastern Canada also. The dairy farmers in Quebec have surplus problems. Some farmers in the Maritimes, some potato farmers and corn producers in Ontario have to sell their production below cost price.
Mr. Speaker, the government does not propose anything to help these farmers. It is good of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture to solve problems, to help and to promise $500 million to the western farmers.
However, this does not complete the farm policy for the whole country. Has the government offered a national farm policy for Canada since it has come to power? Has the previous government ever presented a general farming policy for Canada as a whole?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member will allow me to interrupt him for a moment in order to remind him that the house is presently considering a specific motion. The hon. member should somehow keep in mind the rule of relevancy, and his comments should relate to the motion under consideration at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) allows us to give the reasons why we will support it. The Leader of the Opposition himself blamed the government for its inaction.
The leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) had every chance to come out with what he had to say, and this too is related to the amendment, whereby the house would resume its work at the end of September in order to solve the problems that have been set aside, and which the government or the Prime Minister did not want to put before the house.
Since the beginning of the session we have been asked to adopt bills of very little importance while the government neglected to introduce the important ones. That is why, we will support the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition, so that the house might be invited to meet sooner to enable the government to introduce its legislation. The government has certainly prepared its legislative program because for a year and a half now, we have been hearing of all those steps that have been taken to realize a "just society". So, legislation must be ready. Why wait before putting it before parliament?
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House
Some bills were introduced, namely the omnibus bill, other secondary bills were also put to us. This last month we have been discussing parliamentary procedures. But has that solved the economic problems in Canada?
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, it is important for the members to meet as soon as possible. If this was not urgent, I admit that perhaps we could take a break until October 22. I could even suggest better than that: that sessions always be held at set dates, that the opening of the session be set for such and such a date, the closing or adjournment for Christmas and the New Year be always from December 20 to January 18 or 20 and that the house adjourn in June to come back in September. In summer, the house would adjourn at the end of June or the beginning of July and convene when the school opens early in September, because there are so many school children on the other side and it would be too bad to deprive them of the education they are entitled to.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be appropriate for the government to pass legislation so that sessions should always be within fixed dates. However, owing to circumstances, such is not the case; we are asked to adjourn until October 22. The Leader of the Opposition suggests September 22 so that we may have a month for the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. As the leader of the N.D.P. pointed out, that would take about ten days or about the whole of October. In November we could begin with the bills that were so much promised by the government in the last Speech from the Throne.
Mr. Speaker, in the public interest, I believe it is urgent that we talk for instance about the underdeveloped areas the producers the farmers the overall agricultural policy in Canada, the social security structure that should be amended, old age pensions, pensions to veterans and retired people.
Those matters should be discussed as soon as possible. For three, four years or even five years already, the government has been asked to bring solutions in order to help those pensioners. The minister will say again: We are asked by the opposition to spend more money, but the government has less and less money.
And the Treasury will run dry because precisely the government allows financial sharks
[Mr. CaouetteJ
to increase their interest rates. The government will be supplied by financial sources on which it has to pay accrued interest. If it borrows $1 million or $1 billion on a 12-, 15-or 20-year basis, it would have to pay back $2 billion. And to pay off the second billion, it would have to borrow again, because this is how the system works.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the Creditistes maintain that the first thing to be settled in Canada is the monetary system. The government should introduce in the house a specific, clear and definite legislative program with regard to the Canadian monetary system, which is at the origin of the inflation so often referred to by the Prime Minister. He dealt with it and we are sinking deeper and deeper into inflation which enables the rich to get richer and the poor to get poorer.
This is the system in which we operate and as long as that system controls the destiny of our nation, we will be in the same mess. Whether it be under the government of this Prime Minister or the next one or a former one, we always end up in a dead end and a solution is impossible to find. Such is the situation in which we find ourselves.
The government proposes now the adjournment until October 22nd simply because he has no solution to offer, because he does not have the courage to introduce its legislative program and to suggest solutions to the problems. Let him at least put the problems to the house and we are going to provide it with the solutions Canada needs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment purports to have the session resume on September 22 instead of October 22.
I listened carefully to the interventions of opposition party leaders. I must say that one of them did not surprise me very much. As for the other two, I will deal with them in a moment.
The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste did not surprise me very much. He was never in power and he will never be. He does not know what is a government.
He will never know it.

He will never know it. This position is easy and quite clear. A very long time ago, no doubt when he was still a child, he stated his political theory and economic
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
philosophy. Everything boils down to the monetary system. He found the truth several years ago. He thinks he can stop thinking, studying and examining because he has the answer to everything: the reform of the monetary system. If there is too much pollution it is because of the monetary system. If housing is in a bad way, the monetary system is to blame. Canadian participation abroad also depends on the monetary system, and digestion too, for that matter.
Mr. Speaker, I understand why that party does not need any respite, that it does not need any time to study and do research. In theory, as well as intellectually, they have found out everything. They have only one thing left to do and it is to make the people believe it and for that, of course, they must talk. And in order to do so, they must of course, be in the house. Give them holidays and they vanish out of the picture. They become nobodies-they are just nil.
Hear, hear.

They are here, Mr. Speaker, to be seen and to be heard. They need a forum and there is none except in the house. They do not want to go in their constituencies, because the people there do not want to see them. They have heard the same things over and over again for too many years.
Hear, hear.

Well, they are welcome to stay in Ottawa if they like.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscamingue has a problem. He wants to say a few words on the monetary system.
You say you have no money?
That is always what is missing, dollars!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order!

You mentioned that in
Rouyn, you said you did not have any money.
You also said that in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscamingue and his colleagues of the Ralliement Creditiste might take advantage of the time we are allowing them to study the problems a bit and to examine the solutions we are proposing.
The hon. member has just mentioned my trip in western Canada and, talking through
Motion to Adjourn House his hat as usual, he referred to the solutions we proposed.
He refers to $250 million and $500 million that we are supposed to have thought up as a result of my trip in western Canada. It is not true, Mr. Speaker. It is only a matter of applying a policy already in existence which was misunderstood in the west. As a matter of fact, it is a policy of advance payments on unsold wheat. However, the hon. member did not understand it neither did several Canadians in the west.
That is why we are urging the hon. members to spend a little more time in their constituency in order to explain the policy or solutions that have been misunderstood.
Mr. Speaker, in order to understand and to be in a position to explain, one needs a little silence, a little reflection and a little study. That is asking a lot from the opposition parties, especially from the Creditistes, who have always been in possession of the truth in all fields. They should at least show some indulgence and realize that others are not as blessed and are trying to determine the extent of the problems and to find solutions.
And so, Mr. Speaker, in order to program to some extent the legislative year, we have presented the measures under study. We have implemented a recommendation contained in the report of the Standing Committee on Procedure, presented to the house on December 6 last.

The Committee on Procedure recommended that there be a pattern of regular parliamentary sessions whereby a session would normally commence in September or October and the house would rise for the summer recess on or about July 1. There was no hidden desire on the part of the government to change this. We are following the plan that was proposed by the committee on procedure and about which I spoke in the house on December 10 last. At that time I explained that it was our intention as a government to follow this plan to have a regular legislative year which would begin probably early in October and end late in June. On December 10 I said we thought this was necessary, and I continued:
This would enable the government to complete Its legislative program during the summer months. By the time the house convenes, a substantial number of bills would be ready for first reading. The bulk of the legislative work would be undertaken in the autumn and early winter. The house would be able to concentrate on the main financial work in the spring and to complete it before a
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House summer adjournment. During each of three periods of the proposed annual session a fixed number of days would be set aside for the opposition.
And so on. This was the government's plan. We did not pretend that we had all the bills written up and all the policies defined for four years in advance. We said we would have to do a little bit of thinking and a little bit of reading of the reports which the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) has said are piled up on our desks. It is true that there are many reports we have to study and many policies that we have to think through. We have to give the civil service many directives so they can draft bills and prepare white papers under governmental direction in order that they can be examined by cabinet committees and then by the cabinet. These things take a little time.
I said that the leader of the Creditistes did not surprise me because he did not know much about governing. I am a little more surprised by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the leader of the New Democratic party because they were premiers; they were heads of government in the past. They used to know what it was to govern.
And still do.

What were they doing in those days? I think it would be fair to say that the legislative assembly of Nova Scotia sat perhaps two or three months a year. Why not six? Was it because they did not clear up the mess in their province?

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)

What were they doing in the other eight, nine or ten months of the year? Were they off on vacation, as the leader of the New Democratic party just said? Is it because they wanted to send everybody home to do nothing, or is it because they thought that the purpose of the government was to come to grips with problems and to look for solutions, and that it was necessary for the members of the various political parties to be in their ridings, not only to understand the problems of the ridings but to explain to their parts of the province the problems in other parts?
Then you better give them a whole year to explain it.
Do you want to ask a question?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should be allowed to make his speech.

I would have answered this question if it had been put, but let me tell the hon. member's neighbour, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Macln-nis), not to ask me any questions because I do not answer people who are not gentlemen.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order which arises from the remark of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about not answering my questions. When he does not answer me he does not answer thousands of the constituents whom I represent, but at least he has not threatened to kick me, brown belt and all.
He kicks children only.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member in a moment. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
My
point of order is that I agree completely with you, Mr. Speaker, and I think that our debate will be carried on in a better vein if we do not say of members in the house that any hon. member is not a gentleman.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Without commenting on the point of order, perhaps I might revert to my original thought that we should return to the substance of the motion now before the house.

I was speaking to the amendment, Mr. Speaker. I related the reasons why we need to have a certain period of time between the sessions of this house, and I was saying that I was somewhat surprised that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) did not know about this. It is not so long ago that he was the head of a government in a province which had economic and social
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
problems. Was his solution to these to sit two months a year and send the members home on vacation for the rest of the time and go on vacation himself, or did he have to stay around and do some work? And if ten months were needed for him, why would three months be too much for us?
Hear, hear.

I must say that if both he and the leader of the New Democratic party had sat a little longer than six or eight weeks or even three months, perhaps they would not have left their provinces in such a mess and the federal government would not have to pick up the pieces.
I think we should encourage members of the opposition to leave. Every time they do, the I.Q. of this house rises considerably.
When the Leader of the Opposition rose to speak of truancy, there were only 27 out of the 70 members of his party in the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
And there were only 65 of
your party here at that time.

One of the difficult problems with which we have to deal, and which takes a lot of our time in cabinet committees and in cabinet, and with which the civil service has to come to grips, is the problem of regional economic disparity. Much of this disparity occurs in the province of the Leader of the Opposition, and if he had not left that province in such a mess, if he had done a little more for education and housing, if he had not left the heavy water industry and Clairtone in such a mess, perhaps we would not have to deal with it now, and perhaps the economic situation of the whole region would be better.
But no, they wanted ten months of holiday a year. According to their interpretation of the reason for our three months' recess, we want to send members on vacation. Apparently that is what they did and they think we are doing the same. But we are not; we are not sending members home on vacation. I hope they will take a few weeks' vacation and I hope the ministers will do so also, but we certainly do not intend to take three months' vacation.
Our members of parliament, the members of the Liberal party, do things in their constituencies during the three months' recess.
Hear, hear.

I understand that the government of the leader of the New Democratic party sometimes sat as long as six or eight
Motion to Adjourn House weeks a year. Big deal! But when he is here he really comes to grips with problems. When he is in the opposition, he really knows how to solve problems which he did not know how to solve when he was head of a provincial government. We hear a lot of talk about wheat and about inflation. 1 wonder if the leader of the New Democratic party really did much to solve the problem of wheat when he was premier of Saskatchewan.
Oh, come off it.

When I was there last week I was appalled to see how many friends of his political party were misinformed about wheat problems, how his party has not really helped the people of that province to understand the real nature of the wheat problem, and how they have not helped this wheat growing population to embark on any kind of forecasting or planning in the solution of these problems. I can understand why.
The leader of the New Democratic party says that we are adjourning until October 22 because we want to give our members longer holidays. By virtue of the same reasoning which I applied to the Leader of the Opposition, I suppose that is what they did in Nova Scotia after sitting six or eight long weeks a year. They adjourned to send their members, as he said, on longer holidays. That is not the way we see it.
The opposition seems to think it has nothing else to do but talk. They say: if there is a problem, we will talk. If there is a difficulty, we will talk about it. If the government is going too slowly, we will talk about it. If there is a real problem in some part of Canada, we will talk about it. That is all they have to do. They do not have to govern, they have only to talk. The best place in which to talk, if they want a forum, is, of course, parliament. When they get home, when they get out of parliament, when they are 50 yards from Parliament Hill, they are no longer hon. members-they are just nobodies, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
Oh, oh.

We are quite candid about it. We have to do some thinking. Before solving the problems we have to examine them in depth. They have to be discussed between ministers. We have to get departments to work on them. Sometimes we have to name outside experts or set up task forces to look for solutions. Then we have to take time to
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House discuss them; we have to arrive at policy decisions. Then we have to send them for drafting, whether in the form of white papers or bills.
Macgregor Dawson said all that.
Yes, but you should have read Macgregor Dawson.
I did.
So the hon. member read Macgregor Dawson. Now they have two authorities on which to rely-Macgregor Dawson and the Canada Year Book.
Oh, oh.

Yes, and the Colonial Laws Validity Act.
It is only fair to confess that unlike the leader of the Creditiste party (Mr. Caouette) we did not formulate our solutions for all time 50 years ago, or 60 years ago, I suppose. We have to find new solutions all the time because the problems of Canada are changing. I may say we also have to spend time doing so.
I would suggest that the role of the opposition-and this is perhaps a chapter which the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) did not read-is not merely to talk about everything, not merely to be against anything the government does, not merely to say that our Indian policy is bad, that our position with regard to the Commonwealth is wrong, and that we are failing to stop inflation. This is one of the roles of the opposition, of course, and this is why we have allotted to them under the new rules-
Isn't that kind?

-one quarter of the days in a normal parliamentary session. Hopefully this will give them a little time in which to talk against our policies and criticize our mistakes. But we urge them also to spend a little time trying to become a credible opposition.
We are told that the government has destroyed its credibility, Mr. Speaker. That is possible. We have come forward with policies which perhaps have failed to please everyone in the country. Someone asks, what policies? We have come forth, for instance, with a policy position on the Indian problem. When it was presented to the house I remember distinctly the leaders of all the opposition parties saying: Too late; you should have 
done that years ago; we have been pushing that for years; we told you so. In effect they told us we had adopted their policies, only many years too late.
A few days later, Mr. Speaker, the Indians began saying the policy was not such a good one after all-it is true they had once been against the Indian Affairs department, but now it did not seem so bad. The opposition switched!
Shame.

Suddenly our policy decision, which had been theirs, but which had been adopted ten years too late, was no longer theirs. Somebody in the country was against it. Right away, it was no longer their policy. It was wrong, and it should be reversed.
Perhaps our Indian policy is wrong, Mr. Speaker. We are asking the Indians to discuss it, and we are asking the provinces to discuss it too. Perhaps the Canadian people are not prepared to live without discrimination among themselves. Perhaps the Canadian people think there should be treaties between one section of the Canadian people and another section. Perhaps we shall not be able to succeed in selling what we believe to be the right Indian policy.
But what is the opposition's Indian policy? It was one thing one day, and ten days later it was another. Precisely what it was we do not know. On one day it was years too late and on another it was years too soon. It might not be too much to suggest that in the time between now and September 22 the opposition members should try to meet a few of their constituents who still believe in them, and perhaps they could take a little holiday. But they might take the time between September 22 and October 22, the extra month we are asking hon. members to take as an interval between the two sessions, as time in which to come up with an Indian policy. Possibly it would be better than ours and possibly we could hear about it.
As to the other subjects which have been mentioned, it is true we did not settle all the problems of Canada. We did not pretend we would. But we did bring some propositions forward. For instance, for weeks and months one hon. member kept asking me what we intended to do about offshore mineral rights.
I would say that we hoped to make a statement soon, next month, perhaps, or in two weeks time. Then one day we announced it. And not a word has been heard since then on the subject of offshore mineral rights. Is our
July 25, 1969	COMMONS
position the right one in the estimation of hon. members opposite, or is it wrong? We know that many of the provinces have approved its general lines while others have declined to accept it. The provinces will not get any guidance from the opposition, Mr. Speaker. Apparently they have not had time to think about it or to formulate a policy.
We have heard a great deal from the expert on oil. He has asked us constantly about our oil policy, and about the "secret agreement" which is a figment of his imagination. But what is the policy of the opposition on these complex questions involving offshore mineral rights? Should we divide the revenue-and I am talking now of the share which would accrue to the federal government-among the provinces claiming it, or among all Canadians? Should we divide it on a per capita basis? Should we divide it only among those provinces which have coastlines or should we give part of it to provinces which are already rich in oil, such as Alberta?
These are difficult problems, Mr. Speaker. We proposed some solutions. What are the solutions offered by the opposition? One day they hope to sit on the treasury benches. One day, they say, they will govern this country. And I am sure the first thing they will do is to abolish this infamous rule 75c. Their program is quite set in this respect. We know about that. And there will never be any closure under a Conservative government. I need not talk about any other hypothesis. This is their program. They will go to the people with it-"We shall abolish closure and we shall remove rule 75c".
What will they do about offshore mineral rights? What will they do to settle the Indian problem? What will they do about inflation? I realise I am probably testing your patience a little, Mr. Speaker, and I do not wish to deal at length with any of the issues. However, I want to explain that these are difficult problems
On the subject of inflation we have been asked, I suppose, 50 questions by one hon. member during the course of the year. They were not all in order, Mr. Speaker, but we have at least done something about inflation. We have not cured it, but we have provided for a budgetary surplus this year, the first, I believe, in 12 or 13 years. In order to continue this surplus we will have to do some more cutting. I remember that when we had to cut from our programs the causeway to Prince Edward Island the opposition were up in 29180-735
Motion to Adjourn House arms. They said we should have built that causeway. They told us to forget about the tunnel to Newfoundland, which had never been promised anyway, but the causeway was inviolate.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Prime Minister did suggest that he was testing my patience in this debate, but the Speaker's patience cannot, of course, be tested. I suggest to the Prime Minister, as I did to the previous speaker, that we are not debating the budget or the Speech from the Throne; we are dealing with a motion to adjourn the house. The comments of hon. members should be related at all times to the motion and the amendment before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with you. The only point I was trying to make was that there are going to be some more difficult decisions that we will have to take during the next three months. We need three months because we are faced with the problem of further cuts in expenditure. We have had no guidance as yet from the opposition as to whether we should lay off more civil servants or should cut back on some public works. These are problems that are being dealt with by the government. We have a good deal of work to do. We will be using most of the summer, as I said in my speech on December 10 and to which I referred a moment ago, to prepare sufficient legislative material so that when parliament reconvenes it will progress efficiently in the next session.
Next session we are looking forward to hearing from the opposition not merely negative rejections of our positions but hopefully some constructive ideas that will help us as a government to be better informed to find solutions-not the problems which we can all see, but to find some of the solutions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister answer a question at this point?
Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
During the course of the recess which lies ahead would the Prime Minister mind examining the 69 private members' notices of motions, the 133 private members' public bills and the numerous amendments that were put forward, substantially by members of the opposition, which might give the Prime Minister some guidance in connection with the problems confronting him?
July 25, 1969

Motion to Adjourn House

That is true. I think the hon. gentleman will recognize that in much of our legislation we have tended to incorporate ideas that appeared in private members' bills. However* these are not always bills sponsored by members of the opposition; a great deal are sponsored by private members on the government side.

Before concluding my comments, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if it would be worthwhile to ponder over the considerable attention which the Leader of the Opposition has been giving to gaullism for several days. He constantly speaks about General de Gaulle, his tactics, he sees gaullism everywhere. It seems to me that it is somewhat out-of-date. I feel that this attempt to bring hate and contempt on a country and on its former president is strangely irrelevant. I do not know if-
It is despicable.

Yes, indeed, it is despicable. I would ask the hon. member to count the number of times that his own leader has spoken of gaullism during the past few days and to note in what context he does it. That gaullism means the end of parliamentary government, I agree, but it is his interpretation. But what brings him to compare this policy with that of the government? I do not know.
AE I can say about General de Gaulle is that I did not always agree with his policy, but I will at least pay him this tribute that to my knowledge, he never considered, unlike the Leader of the Opposition, depriving any member of his privileges retroactively.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all listened with interest to the pompous, ghb, condescending lecture that has been delivered to us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I am sure we have aH been interested to learn from the Prime Minister's own lips that nobody, but nobody, in this country knows anything about running a government or a parliament except this self-styled little tin god on wheels. The pomposity of his speech is indicative of why this house finds it impossible to get along as other houses have been able to do, and to work out legislative procedures for the good of parliament and the country as a whole.
I want to join in this debate at this moment to speak to the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and

to say why I believe parhament should not be recessing at the present time for three months. Between one and two o'clock this morning the government brought in by means of closure a guElotine measure that wEl allow it to program parliament, to turn parliament into an assembly Ene. At one end of the pipe you will put in proposed legislation; at the other end you will take out statutes aE polished and ready for proclamation to the people.
The justification for this action on the part of the government is that the opposition has been holding up parhament. In sending parliament home for three months the government is admitting that it has no legislation ready, and wEl have none ready for another three months. This indicates parhament has not been held up in any way, shape or form by the opposition. In fact the opposition has co-operated so well with the government that every piece of legislation that the government has brought forward has been dealt with expeditiously. Now the government has nothing to present to parliament and so wants to send members of parliament home for three months.

ParEa-ment must sit to solve this problem because, as I shall demonstrate in a moment or two, the government's policies have proved a complete failure.
What is the situation today in regard to inflation? By May 1 the increase in the cost of living during the previous 12 months had risen to 4.4 per cent. One month later, on June 1, it had risen to 4.7 per cent. On July 1, the latest date for which we have figures, the increase over the past 12 months was 5.2 per cent. We ask ourselves what is the figure going to be for the 12 months period ending August 1? The answer is that it will probably be close to 6 per cent because right at this moment the cost of living in Canada is rising at a rate of 10 per cent a year.

The first thing I would do to control inflation would be to control the government spending which has doubled in the six years during which this Liberal government has been in power. The answer is yes, because it was actually done in 1962 by the then Conservative government. On June 23, 1962 the government of that day was faced with an international monetary crisis. In order to obtain the international credit which we need to keep the country's currency solvent, we were required to cut $200 million in expenditures immediately. Those expenditures were cut within a period of three days. Cutting $200 million on that date, effective during that present fiscal year, amounted to the same thing as cutting $265 million in a full fiscal year.

Motion to Adjourn House than the Conservative government did in 1962 when it cut its expenditures by $200 million in that fiscal year, during a period of three days. This can be done, and it is necessary that it be done immediately.
The second suggestion I have for controlling the escalating cost of living is to lower prices by increasing productivity. I urge the government, as I have done on many occasions in the past, to bring in tax incentives in order to interest industry in this country to invest in new plant, machinery, and production systems, necessary to cut the cost of production, materially and lower the selling price of goods. This could be done if the government introduced tax incentives. The cost to the treasury would be more than made up-many times over-in subsequent years as a result of greater sales abroad of Canadian products. The lower cost of production would make possible lower selling prices, and this could be brought about by greater productivity.
The third positive suggestion I make to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is that he approach the provinces immediately at a federal-provincial conference with the objective in mind of persuading the provinces to give the federal government the means to impose consumer credit restrictions. As we all know the public today is being bombarded with advertisements urging it to buy anything from a packet of pins to a red convertible, with little or no down payment, and several years to pay. In other words the public today is spending a vast amount of money it does not possess.
We all agree that credit is very necessary to our economy, and reasonable credit should be made available. What I suggest is that unreasonable or ridiculous credit should be avoided. A down payment of at least 25 per cent should be required on purchases that are reasonable, and a payoff period should be allowed depending on the type of product. Today consumer spending is completely out of control, and vast sums of money are being spent that people ini Canada do not possess.
This great increase in the purchasing power of the Canadian people is one of the things pushing up the cost of living. There are inflationary pressures because there is an overdemand for goods resulting from easy credit. As the governor of the Bank of Canada advised the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs a few days ago, consumer credit control would undoubtedly have been imposed by the federal authority

that council he has put all the senior members of his government. This is evidence of the fact that the President of the United States and the United States government consider this to be the No. 1 problem in that country. The problem is just as grave in Canada.

We need a national pollution policy for this reason: It is very difficult for a province to bring in good, tough legislation requiring municipalities to instal the type of machinery costly machinery necessary to deal with pollution. Legislation must be enacted which deals with this problem on provincial borders. For instance if Ontario were to enact a tough law, industries from other countries that might be settling in Canada and looking for a place in which to establish a factory might say, "We shall not go to Ontario because they have tough laws with regard to pollution; therefore we had better go to Quebec, Manitoba, Nova Scotia or somewhere else."
If we are to have the kind of legislation that is necessary to require industries and municipalities to instal the type of machinery that will remove bacteria from waste before it is released into the environment, it must be a national law which applies equally to industries and municipalities in all parts of the country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is responsible-as is President Nixon, who has accepted the responsibility-for calling together the provincial premiers and proposing to them that there be a national law requiring pollution control in their provinces.

I now wish to speak about the matter of poverty in this country. Last August, nearly a year ago, the Economic Council of Canada made available a very valuable report to the Canadian people and the government. It devoted 38 pages to the question of poverty, which it described as a national disgrace. When the Prime Minister was asked whether he agreed with that description he said yes. So the Prime Minister knows that poverty in this country is a national disgrace. The government admits it is a national disgrace, and it came into power pledged to bring in the just society, which should include the elimination of poverty.
On September 13 of last year I asked the Prime Minister whether he would consider increasing the federal minimum wage as an example and inducement to the provincial governments to follow suit and bring minimum wages up to a reasonable level. This is very necessary because, as the report of the Economic Council of Canada pointed out very clearly, poverty does not exist to the greatest extent with people who are on welfare. Those people are usually maintained just above the poverty level. The report pointed out that those suffering poverty in this country are for the most part living on minimum wages, which vary across Canada from 80 cents an hour to $1.30' an hour.
The Prime Minister is making some motions about the time. I am glad that for once he is paying attention to what we have to say. I ask the Prime Minister not to worry about the time; I will look after that. My time is not up; I have a few more minutes, have I not, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext: Prior to recognizing the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) I might perhaps express the misgiving I have. It seems to me that we are getting more and more into what amounts to a budget debate or an address debate, and I think all hon. members appreciate the difficulty in maintaining relevance to an adjournment motion. I appeal however to hon. members to try to relate their remarks to the motion before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your admonition that our comments should be relevant to the motion. That is not very difficult. There are all kinds of arguments and reasons why we should assemble again here on September 22 instead of in October. First there is the business of this nation which is crying for attention, and there are economic circumstances that exist in both western and eastern Canada and which can only be described as unfinished business so far as this house is concerned.
We have spent the better part of a month discussing a procedural question, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself charged the opposition with being stupid even to discuss it. So if we were stupid to discuss it, I wonder what one can say about the government which brought it in. As a result this month, which could have usefully been used to deal with some of the real problems that exist, has been lost. What should have been done has been left undone.
Surely the Prime Minister cannot be unaware of the circumstances existing in western Canada. He went out to have a look, and the people there made him very welcome. If he is out there again on September 22 I am sure they will make him welcome again, because I suspect that the government will have done no more in regard to the conditions that face the western farmer by September 22 than they have done up to this day in July. We
Motion to Adjourn House have had no report from the Prime Minister since we came back. He has not chosen to rise in his place in the house and say, "This is what I saw when I went to visit the people in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta." He did rise today and in the course of his address told the leaders of two opposition parties what he thinks of the kind of shop that they ran when they were in their provinces. I have some sympathy for him and I am sorry that he came to Saskatchewan at the particular time and under the particular circumstances which he did. We have suffered a Liberal government for some five years in that province and what the Prime Minister was seeing were the results of that administration.
All we see is the ineptitude of the federal Liberal government in its marketing policy, as is evidenced in the present situation of western grain farmers. I can understand why his impressions were as they were.
The reason for the real urgency in meeting again a month ahead of the date suggested by the government is that we may have some report on what has been accomplished in regard to the very serious difficulties that face Saskatchewan and western Canada.
Let me point out that as of October 22 we will be about ten days short of a quarter of the new crop year in marketing western grain. We start on that crop year on August 1, and there is no indication from the government, either through the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) or the Prime Minister that they are aware of the depth of the problem in the marketing of western grain. I am speaking not only of wheat. I am speaking also of barley, flax, and rapeseed. There is no indication as yet that the government are aware of the magnitude of the problem they face or that they have put in motion the machinery to deal with that problem. If they have done so, they have not told this house.
The Prime Minister expressed his contempt for the opposition, and for individual members of the opposition. Perhaps this is why he has not felt it necessary to inform people such as myself, who were elected by the voters in Saskatchewan, and who are backbenchers, how the government intends to deal with the problem. He referred to us as nobodies. Fortunately I do not mind it because I know the traditions of this house, and the parliamentary traditions that went before it.
